unit.title: How attacks work, and how to defend

lesson.title: Social engineering: hacking people
lesson.subtitle: The tricks attackers play on feelings, and how to say no

video.title: Social engineering: hacking people
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Classroom at break. Ms Salma holds up a phone showing an incoming call from an unknown number; a speech bubble from the phone reads ‘IT team’.
scenes.animation: Phone rings with a small shake; Salma narrows her eyes.
scenes.narration: “Hi, I’m from the school’s IT team, and I just need your password to fix your account.” That’s what a caller told one of my students last term. He was polite, he knew her name, and he sounded busy. She almost told him.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card: the Darsi mark, the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: social engineering, how attackers trick people instead of computers, and how you stop them.

scenes.visual: Left: a computer behind a thick wall. Right: a smiling person with an open hand. An arrow skips the wall and goes to the person.
scenes.animation: The arrow bounces off the wall, then curves to the person.
scenes.narration: Breaking into a well-protected computer is hard. Tricking a person is often much easier. That’s social engineering: getting someone to hand over a password, a code, money or access, by playing on their feelings.

scenes.visual: Five rows: a badge, a clock, a warning sign, a gift, a question mark.
scenes.animation: Rows slide in as each trick is named.
scenes.narration: Attackers use the same few tricks again and again. Authority: “I’m from IT, the bank, the ministry.” Urgency: “Do it in the next ten minutes.” Fear: “Your account will be banned.” A gift or flattery: “You’re our lucky winner.” And curiosity: a file or a stick you just have to open.

scenes.visual: Four small scenes: a phone call, a game chat bubble, a profile with a borrowed photo, a person with full hands at the computer-room door.
scenes.animation: Scenes flip in one by one.
scenes.narration: It happens everywhere. A phone call from “support”. A message in a game chat from a “moderator”. A new account using a friend’s photo. Or someone who follows you into the computer room because their hands are full.

scenes.visual: A market. A man asks a girl the time; while she looks at her watch, his partner reaches toward her bag. Then the same scene with her hand firmly on the bag.
scenes.animation: Freeze on the reach; the bag slides away.
scenes.narration: Think of a pickpocket in the market who asks you the time. While you look at your watch, his partner reaches for your bag. Social engineers work the same way: they keep your mind busy with a feeling, so you don’t stop to think.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph in the computer room holds up a USB stick with a paper label. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Joseph slides in; the cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! You find a USB stick in the computer room, labelled “Exam answers”. What do you do?

scenes.visual: The ‘hand it to a teacher’ card gets a check badge. The stick goes into Mr Joseph's hand, still in its bag.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the stick slides to Joseph.
scenes.narration: Hand it to a teacher, unopened. The label is the bait: curiosity is exactly what the person who left it is counting on. A planted stick can install malware the moment it’s plugged in.

scenes.visual: Four numbered steps on a card: a pause sign, two phones, a crossed-out key, a speech bubble with ‘No’.
scenes.narration: One defence works against every trick. Slow down: pressure is a warning sign. Check through another channel: call back on a number you already know, or ask a teacher face to face. Never share passwords or codes; real support never needs them. And remember, “no” is always allowed.

scenes.visual: Two columns: real help on the left with a calm clock; a trick on the right with a ticking bomb-like clock and a key.
scenes.animation: Items fill each column in turn.
scenes.narration: How do you tell real help from a trick? Real help lets you take your time and call back. It never asks for your password or a code. A trick rushes you, threatens you, and wants a secret right now.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with an incoming call from ‘IT support’ and three answer buttons.
scenes.animation: The call screen slides up; buttons pop.
scenes.on_screen_text: In the lab: a call from “IT”
scenes.narration: In the lab, you’ll take a call from “IT support” about a virus. Choose what you’d really say, and see which tricks the caller used on you.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up a phone with a game chat open: a message from ‘Moderator’ with a countdown. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. In a game chat, a “moderator” says your account will be banned in ten minutes unless you confirm your password. Real or a trick?

scenes.visual: The ‘trick’ card gets the check badge. Three summary cards line up: a pause hand, two phones, a crossed-out key.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: A trick: a deadline, a threat and a password request, all in one message. Remember: feel the pressure, pause, check another way, and never share a password or a code.

scenes.visual: A family at dinner; a student explains with her hands; a parent nods and holds up a phone. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Speech bubbles pop; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: tell someone at home about these tricks. Agree on one family rule: nobody shares a code or a password, whoever asks. And if a call feels wrong, hang up and call back on a number you know.

checkpoints.prompt: You find a USB stick in the computer room labelled “Exam answers”. What do you do?

options.text: Plug it in to see what’s on it
Don’t plug it in: hand it to a teacher
Check it at home on a family laptop

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a stick left as bait can install malware the moment it’s opened. Let the school deal with it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the label is the bait. A planted stick can install malware on any computer, at school or at home. Hand it to a teacher.

checkpoints.prompt: In a game chat, a “moderator” says your account will be banned in 10 minutes unless you confirm your password. Real or a trick?

options.text: A trick — it rushes you and wants your password

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a deadline, a threat and a password request together are a trick. Real moderators never ask for your password.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — moderators can ban accounts, but they never need your password. The rush and the threat are the trick.
